report.tagline: The BBC's free-to-watch streaming app for UK homes, paid for by the TV licence fee instead of ads or subscriptions.
report.simpleSummary: BBC iPlayer is the BBC's app for watching its TV channels live and on demand: shows like Doctor Who, EastEnders, Traitors and live sport like Wimbledon. There are no ads and no monthly subscription. Instead, every UK home that watches live TV or uses iPlayer must buy a yearly TV licence, which costs £180 from April 2026. You need to sign in, and you must confirm you have a licence.

keyNumbers.note: Reported by GB News and others; it was £174.50 in 2025/26 and £169.50 in 2024/25.

overview.whatItDoes: iPlayer lets UK viewers stream BBC channels live, catch up on shows and watch box sets, on phones, laptops, smart TVs and consoles. It is paid for by the TV licence, not ads. The BBC is a public service broadcaster, so its goals are reach and value for licence payers, not profit.
howItWorks: Users create a free BBC account with a UK postcode and confirm they have a TV licence.
They can watch all BBC channels live, and most programmes for up to a year or more after broadcast.
Box sets and archive shows sit alongside new programmes.
Live events like Wimbledon, the Euros and Glastonbury stream with extra streams not shown on TV.
The BBC uses viewing data to personalise rows and recommend shows.
It only works in the UK; overseas viewers are blocked.
overview.valueProposition: For UK viewers: high-quality British TV, news and live events, with no ads and no extra monthly fee beyond the licence. For the BBC: a way to stay relevant as people stop watching live TV.

coreFeatures.whyItMatters: The core reason people use it, and it keeps the BBC relevant to non-live viewers.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Full series of popular shows and archive content.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Competes with Netflix for binge-watching time.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Uses sign-in data to recommend shows.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Helps people find more of what the BBC makes, which drives reach.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Extra live streams for sport and music events.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Shows the BBC's public-service value at big national moments.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Asks users to confirm they hold a TV licence.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Protects licence fee income, the BBC's main money.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Lets users download shows on phones and tablets to watch offline.

businessModel.summary: iPlayer does not make money directly. Every UK home that watches live TV or uses iPlayer must pay a yearly licence fee of £180. That money funds the BBC's content and services, including iPlayer. BBC Studios sells BBC shows abroad and earns extra money. The big problem is that fewer homes are paying.

revenueStreams.detail: £180 a year per household, about £3.8 billion in 2024/25, collected by TV Licensing.
Sells BBC shows and formats like Bluey and Strictly abroad, and runs BritBox International; about £2.2 billion of revenue.
Smaller funding for the World Service.

businessModel.pricing: Free to use for UK homes with a TV licence. The licence costs £180 a year from April 2026 (black and white licence is cheaper). Fines of up to £1,000 apply for watching without one.
costDrivers: Making TV shows, news and sport
Collecting the licence fee and enforcement
businessModel.unitEconomics: Each paying household gives the BBC £180 a year, or £15 a month, about the same as a Netflix Standard plan. That money pays for all of the BBC: TV, radio, news, websites and iPlayer. The problem is that each lost licence takes away £180 a year, and about 540,000 licences were lost in a single year, roughly £97 million. Since it costs little extra to stream to one more home, keeping households paying matters far more than cutting costs per viewer.

howTheyGetUsers: BBC One and other channels promoting iPlayer shows
National moments like the Olympics, Wimbledon and Christmas specials
Hit shows like The Traitors and Gladiators
Pre-installed on most UK smart TVs and set-top boxes
whatBringsUsersBack: Weekly new episodes of dramas and soaps
Box sets released all at once
growth.moat: The BBC has nearly 100 years of trusted brand and British content, plus funding that does not depend on ads. No other service gets guaranteed money from most UK homes. But that money is shrinking, and young people are less attached to the brand.

northStar.metric: Weekly signed-in households watching at least 30 minutes on iPlayer
northStar.why: As a north star metric, this shows how many licence-paying homes get real value from the BBC each week. That value is what keeps households willing to pay.

strengths: Trusted brand and high-quality British content
Big national events and live news
weaknesses: Depends on a licence fee that fewer homes pay
Smaller budget than Netflix or Amazon for big dramas
risks: Licence fee model breaking as people stream instead of watching live TV
Charter renewal by 2027 could change funding to a subscription or tax
Editorial controversies, such as the 2025 Panorama edit that led to the director general leaving
Competition for young viewers from YouTube and TikTok
userComplaints: Having to pay £180 a year even if you watch little BBC
Licence checks and plans to link accounts to home addresses feel intrusive
Concerns about bias and editorial mistakes

improvementIdeas.idea: Monthly licence payments through the iPlayer app with one tap.
improvementIdeas.problem: Many young people drop the licence because £180 feels like a big one-off bill.

improvementIdeas.idea: Young adult section built from BBC Three, comedy and creators, with Shorts-style clips.
improvementIdeas.problem: Young viewers prefer YouTube and TikTok.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: More weekly reach among 16 to 34 year olds.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Weekly reach among 16 to 34 year olds

improvementIdeas.idea: Show each user a yearly 'what your licence gave you' summary.
improvementIdeas.problem: People do not see the value they get from the BBC.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Better perception of value and renewals.

improvementIdeas.idea: Easier TV sign-in via a QR code and phone.
improvementIdeas.problem: Older users struggle to sign in on TVs.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Sign-in completion rate on smart TVs

improvementIdeas.idea: Keep the most-watched box sets available for longer through BBC Studios deals.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: More watch time and better satisfaction.

pmLessons: Funding shapes the product. A licence-funded service must prove value to everyone, not just maximise profit.
Forcing people to sign in gives you data but adds friction; make it as easy as possible.
Habits shift. As viewers moved from live TV to apps and YouTube, the BBC's old payment model weakened.
Trust is a product feature. Editorial mistakes hurt the BBC's reason to exist.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you get more under-35s using iPlayer?
interviewQuestions.hint: Understand where they spend time. Propose content, formats and distribution like YouTube. Measure weekly reach.

interviewQuestions.question: Should the BBC replace the licence fee with a subscription for iPlayer?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare reach, revenue, fairness and public value. Think about who would pay and who would leave.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you reduce licence fee evasion using the product?
interviewQuestions.hint: Balance enforcement with user trust and privacy. Use easier payments and value reminders.

interviewQuestions.question: What should iPlayer's north star metric be?
interviewQuestions.hint: It has no ad or subscription revenue, so focus on value to the public, like weekly reach and time spent. Add guardrails.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature for older viewers using iPlayer on TV.
interviewQuestions.hint: Find pains: sign-in, navigation, finding live channels. Propose simple fixes and success metrics.

glossary.meaning: A yearly fee that UK homes must pay to watch live TV or use iPlayer.
When a home watches live TV or iPlayer without paying for a licence.
The legal agreement with the UK government that sets the BBC's purpose and funding, renewed about every ten years.
A broadcaster funded to serve the public interest, not mainly to make profit.
The one number a company uses to judge if it is giving real value to users.
The number of signed-in accounts that watched at least once in a week.
How many different people use a service in a period.

assumptions: iPlayer user and stream numbers are from 2024/25 because the 2025/26 figures were not found.
Licences in force (about 23.3 million) is our estimate from reported falls.
The 1 in 8 evasion figure comes from a news report and may be measured differently by the BBC.
Revenue lost per licence uses the full £180 fee and ignores concessions.
